title: How To Command Respect From Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explores why some teachers seem to manage classrooms almost effortlessly, arguing the difference lies less in the classroom management plan itself and more in how a teacher communicates verbally and non-verbally. He draws an analogy to Cesar Millan's ability to command an unfamiliar dog's respect within seconds through presence alone, suggesting students similarly read a teacher's bearing the moment they enter a room. The article lists ten concrete practices for commanding respect, including confident body language, moving deliberately rather than rushing, being decisive, pausing before speaking, following through on commitments, practicing brevity, staying calm, listening, being prepared, and radiating confidence. Linsin frames these behaviors as learnable habits rather than innate traits, closing with the observation that most students are craving a leader worth following.
points: Students sense within moments of a teacher's entrance whether that teacher is genuinely in charge.
Confident, unhurried body language and a decisive manner project authority more effectively than volume or force.
Pausing until every student is attentive before speaking increases the weight and impact of instructions.
Consistently following through on commitments, especially the classroom management plan, earns lasting respect.
Most students want a leader to look up to and will respond strongly to a teacher who projects genuine confidence.
quotes: Students, too, know whether you’re in charge or not as soon as you enter the classroom. The way you present yourself in front of them has a profound effect on their behavior and the ease in which you are able to manage your classroom.
Rushing around creates negative, excitable energy and makes you appear as if you’re not in control. Work on moving efficiently and gracefully.
Always wait until every student is attentive and looking at you before giving instructions. This shifts control to you and adds more importance to whatever you say.
Do exactly what you say you will do, especially when it comes to your classroom management plan. Your students will respect this above all else.

Like dogs, children can sense fear a mile away and will prey upon it if given the opportunity. If you’re feeling unsure of yourself, practice confident body language until you begin to feel it on the inside.

On the other hand, most students are craving for a leader, for someone to look up to. So when a teacher comes into their life that displays the qualities they respect, they bend over backwards trying to please her/him.
